newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers' blockade shows signs of fraying.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers' blockade shows signs of fraying.

text.p: A road blockade that has nearly paralysed Greece for 16 days showed signs of fraying on Friday but farmers vowed to strengthen barricades cutting the country in half.

Farmers in the central city of Larissa, the hub of the protest, toughened their stance, saying they would not budge until the socialist government met all their demands -- cheaper fuel and equipment, and state subsidies on products.
But Greek media reported barricades around the northern city of Salonika were being abandoned or weakening and only one road block remained on the road to the western port city of Patras.

The government has rejected their demands, saying their cost would distance Greece from its European Union convergence goals. It has ruled out police intervention and appears determined to wait out the crippling blockade.
"We appeal to all to come and start a national dialogue. Let's sit down and talk on Monday," Deputy Development Minister Anna Diamantopoulou told television.
Commerce and industry have warned the damage to Greece's struggling economy from the blockade could be irreversible and have appealed for a settlement.

Exporters, hoteliers and industrialists put losses at more than $500 million. The Association of Northern Greek Exporters said exports had dropped by 42 percent in December as a result of the closing of the borders with Turkey and Bulgaria.
"Our earnings have dropped by 80 percent compared to this time last year," said Christos Folias, president of the Salonika chamber of trade.
In the first sign of easing, farmers on Thursday allowed some foreign truckers drive through their barricades.

"We opened the roadblocks for two hours as a gesture of good will to foreign truck drivers. But our struggle continues and as of tonight nothing will get through," said Thanassis Nasikas, a farmers' representative.
Thousands of tractors have been blocking about 100 key junctions, paralysing overland transport throughout the country, and makeshift camps have appeared alongside the highways.
About 700 foreign trucks have been stranded, with drivers -- mostly British, Dutch, Bulgarian and Turkish -- complaining of lack of food, water and proper sanitation.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis, facing his first crisis since winning elections in September, fears that giving in to the farmers could snowball, with other sectors hard hit by next year's austerity budget taking similar action.
"Demands for billions of drachmas cannot be satisfied. To do so would be a step backwards," he said earlier this week, before flying to Dublin for the EU summit.
During the summit he will be working with a skeleton diplomatic staff, since Greek diplomats have joined several other sectors in striking against tough economic measures.
Diplomats, among the worst paid in the EU, are fighting the taxation of their allowances while posted abroad.
Port workers, teachers, state doctors, customs and taxation employees are either striking or plan strikes until December 19, when parliament votes on the budget.
Boisterous protest marches are an almost daily feature in Athens and Greece's the two biggest labour confederations have called a one-day nationwide strike for December 17.
The budget, aimed to set the course for Greece to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 2001, cuts state hiring, abolishes most tax exemptions and imposes new levies.
